name: Cannabis and gun ownership (federal)
where_it_stands: Federal law still bars unlawful drug users from having guns, but on 18 June 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held that prosecuting a regular marijuana user solely for possessing a gun at home violated the Second Amendment. ATF has proposed a revised Form 4473 that would stop treating state-licensed medical use as unlawful, but that form is not final.

next_milestone.text: ATF final rule on the revised Form 4473 (comment period closed 6 August 2026); no publication date announced.

summary: Under 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(3), an 'unlawful user of or addicted to' a controlled substance may not possess firearms. In United States v. Hemani the Supreme Court affirmed dismissal of a charge against a man who used marijuana about every other day, finding the government's historical analogy to 'habitual drunkard' laws did not support disarming him without evidence he was dangerous; the Court said its ruling is narrow and does not address addicts, people who are intoxicated, or prosecutions with individualized proof of danger. Separately, ATF proposed on 8 May 2026 to revise Form 4473, and NORML reports the draft drops language calling medical marijuana use unlawful while keeping the bar on recreational use. A compliance firm reports ATF has marked its 2011 open letter on medical marijuana cards as rescinded.

what_changes.text: State medical patients may gain a path to buy firearms once a revised form is final; until then the current form still asks about all marijuana use and a false answer is a separate crime.
Adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I and the statute is unchanged; Hemani limits prosecutions based on use alone but does not legalize gun possession by users.

Gun dealers should no longer treat a medical card alone as automatic grounds to deny a sale, according to FFLGuard, but must still deny when they have reasonable cause to believe a buyer is prohibited.

timeline.event: Supreme Court hears argument in United States v. Hemani
ATF publishes proposed Form 4473 revisions, with comments due 6 August
Supreme Court rules 9-0 that Hemani's prosecution violated the Second Amendment
FFLGuard reports ATF has marked its 2011 medical-marijuana open letter as rescinded

faq.q: Can medical marijuana patients own guns under federal law?
faq.a: The statute still bars unlawful drug users. ATF's proposed form would treat state-licensed medical use differently, but it is not final, so patients should get legal advice before buying.

faq.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Hemani?
faq.a: It held that charging a man solely because he regularly used marijuana and kept a gun at home violated the Second Amendment, while leaving other uses of the law open.

faq.q: Does Form 4473 still ask about marijuana?
faq.a: Yes. Until a revised form is adopted, the current form asks about unlawful use of marijuana or any controlled substance.
